name: @ploa/cli

tools.name: ploa_setup_guide
tools.description: Start here for a new app, or when the stores or Ploa aren't set up yet; for an update it says what a store turned down that the person reads and answers. Works out where this folder stands (signed in, app IDs in the Expo config or, for a Flutter, React Native, Capacitor, Gradle or Xcode app, in its own projects, linked to Ploa, each store connected, the app created in each store, signing, store page, first build, Google Play's way to production) and returns what's next, in order: who does each step (the person or you), exactly what to do, and direct links that open the exact page in App Store Connect, Play Console, Apple's developer site and Ploa wherever Ploa knows the IDs. Until the person has chosen how you work (an autonomous agent, or approvals), it opens with that question for you to ask them; ploa_access records the answer. When the app has no bundle ID or package name yet, suggests a few to choose from and explains how the stores treat them. Read-only; run it again after each step.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_link
tools.description: Links the app in this folder to Ploa, like `ploa init`: an Expo app, or a Flutter, React Native, Capacitor, Android (Gradle) or Xcode app. Finds the app in Ploa by its bundle ID or package name, or adds it with the workspace's App Store and Google Play connections, and writes ploa.json (the app's Ploa ID and server, no secrets; fine to commit). Needs ios.bundleIdentifier or android.package in the Expo config, or an applicationId in Gradle / a bundle ID in the Xcode project. With several connections for a store, name one with apple or google.

apple.description: The App Store connection's name, when there are several.

google.description: The Google Play connection's name, when there are several.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_preflight
tools.description: Checks this Expo app for what App Store Connect and Google Play would reject, before spending time on a build (a Flutter, React Native, Capacitor, Gradle or Xcode app, which Ploa builds too, isn't checked yet: it says so, and the build can go ahead): version and build numbers against the stores, bundle IDs, the icon, iOS purpose strings, privacy manifest, export compliance, Play's target SDK, sensitive permissions, and secrets committed to git. Returns each finding with how to fix it.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_build_files_push
tools.description: Finds the files a build on GitHub reads that git doesn't have (the app config's googleServicesFile for Android and iOS, and the .env files Expo loads) in this checkout, and sends those that aren't in Ploa yet or differ from its copy (or the paths given). They wait sealed in Ploa's vault until the person approves them on ploa.dev with one tap; not approved within 24 hours, they're dropped. Tell the person to approve, with the link this returns, and follow it with ploa_approval_status. The files' values never pass through here: only names, sizes and a .env's variable names. Signing and store keys are never build files (Ploa keeps them already). google-services.json and GoogleService-Info.plist aren't secret, so committing them is the other way.

paths.description: Files to send, relative to the app's folder. Default: those the build will miss.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_access
tools.description: Who this Ploa token belongs to and what it may do: its access level (read, draft, submit, production), whether its owner made it autonomous (then App Review, production, prices, testers and products go straight through instead of waiting for a person's approval), and how the person chose this agent works. choose records the person's answer to ploa_setup_guide's first question, and only theirs: "approvals" (each review, release and price change waits for their OK in Ploa) is kept at once; "autonomous" is only asked for: it returns a link where the person, signed in to Ploa, confirms it for this agent (an agent can never make itself autonomous). Without choose it only reads.

choose.description: The person's answer: how this agent works from now on.

tools.name: ploa_usage_get
tools.description: What the workspace uses of its Ploa plan: the plan, apps and members against its counts, this month's cloud builds on Ploa's machines per platform (included, used, left, and what one past the count costs: on Free builds stop at the count, on paid plans each one past it adds to the next bill), and the web's hosting room (sites, storage, traffic). Read it before a build on Ploa's machines (where: "cloud"), adding an app or inviting a member, and tell the person first when it would cost them or stop. Builds on this machine, on GitHub, in Xcode Cloud or in the person's Google Cloud never count here. Read-only: it buys and changes nothing.

tools.name: ploa_status
tools.description: Shows what App Store Connect and Google Play have for this app right now: recent iOS builds and their processing state, App Store versions, and Google Play tracks with their releases and rollout.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_release_start
tools.description: Builds the app and sends it to testers: iOS to TestFlight (signed with the certificate Ploa issues for this build), Android to Google Play internal testing (Ploa signs it with the upload key it keeps). By default it builds on this machine; where: "github" builds on GitHub instead, from the commit on the app's release branch (or sha), with the workflow Ploa wrote for the repo (the app's GitHub card in Ploa sets it up): Android on GitHub's Linux runners, iOS on the person's own Mac registered as a self-hosted runner with the label ploa (it waits for that runner), or on GitHub's Macs where an owner allowed them for the app on its GitHub card. GitHub counts these builds' minutes on the person's own GitHub account (free on a public repository; on a private one a Mac minute counts as ten of the plan's free monthly minutes, about 150 to 200 for an iOS build): say so before building iOS on GitHub's Macs. where: "cloud" builds on Ploa's own machines, from what's pushed to the app's linked GitHub repository, with nothing to set up and nothing counted on GitHub: each plan has a number of cloud builds a month; on Free each one waits a few minutes in a shared queue behind paid plans' builds, and stops at the month's count (say so, and that builds here or on GitHub never count); paid plans go first in line, and builds past the count add to the next bill (say so first). The answer says its place in the queue. where: "xcode-cloud" (iOS only) has Apple build and sign it in Xcode Cloud, from what's pushed to a branch (main unless branch names another), with the app's Xcode Cloud workflow; it needs that workflow made once in Xcode (ploa xcode-cloud in the app's folder says how) and counts against the person's Xcode Cloud hours with Apple. where: "gcp" (Android only) builds with Cloud Build in the workspace's own Google Cloud project, from what's pushed to the app's linked GitHub repository; an owner sets the project up once in Ploa's Settings › Builds (it says what to run in Cloud Shell), and Google bills its build-minutes to that project, never Ploa: the free tier's machine is free for 2,500 minutes a month but slow for Gradle (half an hour or more), and a bigger machine the workspace picked costs per minute from the first one (say which before building). Ploa still signs the bundle: no key goes to Google. On GitHub, in the cloud, in Xcode Cloud and in Google Cloud it builds what's committed and pushed, not local changes. where: "auto" builds on GitHub when that platform is ready there (ploa_github_status), else on this machine, and says which and why. It runs in the background, since a build takes minutes and Apple's processing up to half an hour, and returns a release ID right away; follow it with ploa_release_status. The build number is the next free one unless you pass one. Run ploa_preflight first. This never goes to App Review or production: those need ploa_release_submit_review or ploa_release_promote, and a person's approval.

buildNumber.description: iOS build number or Android versionCode. Default "auto": one higher than anything the store has. On GitHub always "auto".

where.description: Where to build: "here" (this machine, the default), "github" (from what is pushed; iOS on the person's self-hosted Mac runner, or GitHub's Macs if an owner allowed them), "cloud" (Ploa's machines, from what is pushed; counted against the plan's cloud builds), "xcode-cloud" (iOS in Apple's Xcode Cloud, from a pushed branch), "gcp" (Android in the workspace's own Google Cloud project with Cloud Build, from what is pushed; Google bills that project) or "auto" (GitHub when it's ready for this platform, else here).

sha.description: On GitHub, in the cloud or in Google Cloud: the commit to build. Default: the head of the app's release branch.

branch.description: In Xcode Cloud: the branch to build. Default "main".

workflow.description: In Xcode Cloud: the workflow's name, when the app has more than one.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_release_status
tools.description: Where a release stands: building, uploading, being processed by Apple, on TestFlight or internal testing, or failed and why. While it builds on this machine, includes the last lines of the build log.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

tools.name: ploa_release_changes
tools.description: The pull requests merged and the commits between two releases, from the app's GitHub repo (linked on its GitHub card in Ploa): for a release, since the release of its platform before it; with no release, what the release branch has had since the live version (or else the last release that reached testers). Each PR comes with its title, author and description. Use it to write release notes from what people did rather than commit messages alone (the write_release_notes prompt).

releaseId.description: A release. Left out: the app's release branch since the live version.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_release_submit_review
tools.description: Asks a person to approve submitting an iOS build that is on TestFlight for App Review; the in-app products that are ready to submit go to review with it. When the version is already with App Review with an older build, this is refused and says so; replace: true then asks for both steps under one approval: Ploa withdraws the version from App Review, puts this build on it and submits it (App Review starts over). When App Review rejected the version, this sends it back, with this build (a newer one or the same): Ploa puts it on the version and resubmits the submission App Review sent back, as App Store Connect's Resubmit to App Review does, so never do that by hand there; if App Review rejected something else in that submission too (an in-app event, a product page), it says so, and the person fixes or removes it in App Store Connect first. It never waits for a reply to App Review: a rejection that asked for a fix goes back without any text (the fix is the answer), and when App Review's message asks for an answer, the request says so before the person approves, as the thread closes once the version goes back. With replyId (a reply to App Review's message drafted with ploa_app_review_reply), Ploa first puts that reply in the version's App Review Information › Notes, under the same approval, so App Review reads it with the resubmission. Nothing is sent to Apple until a person approves on the Ploa dashboard; this returns at once with the request's ID, so check it with ploa_approval_status. Needs a token allowed to submit.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

replace.description: The version is with App Review with another build: withdraw it and submit this build in its place, under one approval.

replyId.description: A reply to App Review's message for this version, from ploa_app_review_reply: Ploa puts it in the version's App Review notes before submitting.

tools.name: ploa_release_withdraw_review
tools.description: Asks a person to approve taking an iOS version out of App Review (App Store Connect's Remove from review): Ploa cancels its review submission and waits until Apple shows the version as Developer Rejected, editable again, with its build still on TestFlight. Pass the release of any build of that version. To send a newer build in its place in one step, use ploa_release_submit_review with replace: true instead. Nothing changes at Apple until a person approves on the Ploa dashboard; check it with ploa_approval_status. Needs a token allowed to submit.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

tools.name: ploa_release_stop
tools.description: Stops a build that's still building, wherever it runs (GitHub, Ploa's machines, the person's Google Cloud, Xcode Cloud, or a computer with the CLI), as the Stop button on the dashboard does. Like the dashboard, it takes two steps: called without confirm, it changes nothing and says what the build is and what stopping does where it runs; show that to the person, and only once they say yes, call again with confirm: true. Without releaseId it picks the app's newest build that's still building. A stopped build can't be picked up again; the dashboard and ploa_runs show it as stopped by you. A web version still going up to its testing address stops the same way: pass webVersion (its build number) and site. Needs a token allowed to make drafts.

releaseId.description: The build's release ID (ploa_runs lists them). Defaults to the app's newest build still building.

webVersion.description: A web version to stop instead: its build number (ploa_web_status lists them).

site.description: With webVersion: the site's address, when the workspace has more than one.

confirm.description: true only after the person said yes to stopping it.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_release_promote
tools.description: Asks a person to approve moving an Android release from internal testing to production (or beta / alpha; a Wear OS, TV, Automotive or XR build on its form factor's own tracks), optionally as a staged rollout to a percentage of users. Nothing changes on Google Play until a person approves on the Ploa dashboard; this returns at once with the request's ID, so check it with ploa_approval_status. Needs a token allowed to touch production. On the App Store, an approved version is released with ploa_appstore_release, and its phased release changed with ploa_appstore_phased_release.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

track.description: production, beta or alpha. A Wear OS, Google TV, Android Automotive or Android XR build stays on its own form factor's tracks (wear:production…) by itself; name one (wear:production) to choose.

rolloutPercent.description: Share of users for a staged rollout, 1 to 100. Default 100.

tools.name: ploa_rollout
tools.description: Asks a person to approve a change to an Android release's staged rollout on production (or the track it's on): increase to a bigger percentage, halt it (people who have it keep it; no one new gets it), resume a halted one at a percentage, or complete it (everyone). Use it when ploa_quality shows crashes or ANRs rising after a release (halt), or when the rollout looks healthy (increase or complete). Nothing changes on Google Play until a person approves (an autonomous agent's request goes straight through); follow the answer with ploa_approval_status. A first rollout to production is ploa_release_promote. For the App Store's phased release use ploa_appstore_phased_release.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

percent.description: For increase and resume: the share of users, 1 to 99 (complete is 100).

tools.name: ploa_build_diagnose
tools.description: Says why a build failed, as one cause and the step that fixes it, instead of a log: from the newest failed run of this app (or releaseId), and, when given, the build's log (logPath, a file on this computer, or text pasted from GitHub's or Cloud Build's log). It knows the usual ones: disk or memory, the Gradle wrapper committed from Windows, the JDK or Android SDK, CocoaPods, an old Xcode, signing and capabilities, a build number already used, Google Play's target SDK, missing node modules or Flutter, build files git doesn't have, GitHub's billing, and the network or a busy store. A transient one says so: start the same build again with ploa_release_start (say first when it costs the person minutes). When it doesn't know the failure, it says so and gives the error to read.

releaseId.description: The failed release, as ploa_runs lists them. Default: this app's newest failed run.

logPath.description: Absolute path to the build's log on this computer (the CLI prints it: full log: …).

text.description: The end of a log, pasted (GitHub Actions, Cloud Build).

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_runs
tools.description: Lists this app's recent release runs, newest first: each release Ploa carried (started from the CLI, an agent or the dashboard) with its state, who started it, when, how long it took to reach TestFlight or internal testing, the commit, and every step with its duration (build, upload, App Store Connect or signing, Apple processing or Google Play, the testing track, and the App Review or promotion step a person approves). Use it to see why a release failed or where it is.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_shipping_report
tools.description: One report of where this app stands everywhere, like the dashboard's Shipping page: the newest TestFlight build and App Store version, Google Play's testing and production tracks with the rollout, what waits for a person's approval, and the last release run. Read-only. Start here when asked how the app is doing or what to do next.

fresh.description: Ask the stores again instead of using recent copies.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_quality
tools.description: How stable the app's released versions are, from the stores themselves. Read-only. Google Play: the user-perceived crash and ANR rates over 28 days, overall and per version code, against Play's bad-behavior thresholds (1.09% crashes, 0.47% ANRs), and the crashes and ANRs people hit most. App Store: Apple's API has no crash rates, so it gives what Apple offers: Xcode's performance metrics per version (launch time, hangs, memory, disk writes…) with Apple's regressions, and each build's diagnostics (hangs, disk writes, launches). Give releaseId (or platform and version) to check one release before promoting it or widening its rollout; leave them out for the whole app.

releaseId.description: The release ID that ploa_release_start returned.

version.description: Android: the version code. iOS: the build number.

versionName.description: iOS: the version the build belongs to, like 1.2.0.

fresh.description: Ask the stores again instead of the copy from the last half hour.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_appstore_price_points
tools.description: Every price Apple offers in the app's base territory, cheapest first (0 is free), each with the pricePointId that ploa_details_save takes for step price.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_appstore_register_bundle_id
tools.description: For a new app: registers its iOS bundle ID with Apple (nothing happens if it's already there), so the person only picks it when creating the app in App Store Connect, which only a person can do there. Needs a token allowed to submit.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_android_upload_key_get
tools.description: Whether Ploa holds this app's Android upload key, the key every Android build is signed with before it goes to Google Play: its alias, SHA-256 fingerprint and expiry, and its certificate (public) as PEM. The key itself never leaves Ploa. Pass certificatePath to save the certificate there, for a person to give Play Console when it asks for one (Test and release › App integrity › Upload key › Request upload key reset).

certificatePath.description: Absolute path to save the certificate (.pem) to. Optional.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_android_upload_key_save
tools.description: Gives Ploa this app's Android upload key, which it keeps in its vault and signs every Android build with; it never leaves Ploa. how create: Ploa makes a new key (RSA 2048, valid 30 years) right in the vault, so no one holds a copy and no password passes through you. Use it only when Google Play has no upload key for this app yet (a new app, or one never uploaded): Play takes the first build's key as the upload key. how upload: an existing keystore (.keystore, .jks or .p12 in PKCS#12 format) from an absolute path on this machine, with its password and, if it holds several keys, the alias. Use it when Play already knows an upload key, for example one EAS or Android Studio made; take the password from the person or where they keep it, never write it into a file. A key Ploa already holds is replaced only with replace: true, and only when the person asked for it, since Play rejects builds signed with a key it doesn't know. Only a person, or an agent its owner made autonomous (see ploa_access), may do this; the workspace's owners are told each time.

path.description: how upload: absolute path to the keystore.

alias.description: how upload: the key's alias, if the keystore holds several.

replace.description: Replace the upload key Ploa already holds. Only when the person asked.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_get
tools.description: One in-app product or subscription as its store has it: kind, state, name and description per language, the US price, a subscription's period and free trial, on the App Store its subscription group, review note, Family Sharing and image (the one the App Store shows with it: url, Apple's state; Google Play keeps none), and under review what the store still needs before it can go to people and the next step (submit or activate). platform is ios or android; a Google Play subscription's productId is "product:basePlan", as the purchases list shows it. With no productId, what a new one needs: the store's primary language, the languages it takes, and the App Store's subscription groups.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_save
tools.description: Creates an in-app product or subscription in one store (leave productId out and put it in values), or changes one, straight to the store (needs a token allowed to submit). values: kind (subscription, consumable, non_consumable; on create), productId (on create: Apple takes letters, numbers, periods, underscores; Play lowercase), price (US dollars such as "4.99": Apple picks its nearest price point at or above, Play converts it for every country), period (subscriptions: P1W P1M P2M P3M P6M P1Y), trial (P3D P1W P2W P1M, or null to remove), listings ({ locale: { name, description } } in the store's own codes; Hebrew is "he" at Apple, "iw-IL" at Play; Apple names take 35 characters and descriptions 55, Play 55 and 200), and on the App Store referenceName, group (an existing group ID from ploa_product_get) or groupName (a new group), reviewNote, familySharable; on Play basePlanId. From an agent, a new product, a price or a free trial waits for a person's approval, since it sets what people pay; names and notes go straight through. An App Store subscription's price or free trial is set country by country and takes a few minutes: it answers with a job, which ploa_product_job follows.

productId.description: The product to change; leave out to create.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_job
tools.description: How far a long product write got (an App Store subscription's price, free trial or introductory offer, set country by country): its step (prices, trial_remove, trial, intro_remove, intro), how many of how many countries are done, and at the end what the store has now, or why it failed. Ask again every 20 seconds or so until state is done or failed.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_submit
tools.description: Sends one product on its way to people: on the App Store to App Review (Apple takes an app's first products only with a version; then it goes when the version is submitted through Ploa, which sends every ready product along with the version anyway). An approved App Store product's changed names or image are a new version of it (ploa_product_get's version.draft), sent the same way while the approved one stays on sale. On Google Play, puts it on sale. ploa_product_get says first what the store still needs under review.missing (listing, price, screenshot, groupName). From an agent this always waits for a person's approval.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_review_screenshot
tools.description: Uploads the screenshot App Review looks at for one App Store product (PNG or JPEG, up to 10 MB, from an absolute path on this machine): the screen where it's bought in the app. It replaces the one there. Needs a token allowed to submit.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_product_image
tools.description: Uploads the image the App Store shows with one product (where it's promoted, and on its page): PNG or JPEG of exactly 1024×1024 pixels, up to 10 MB, from an absolute path on this machine. It replaces the one there and goes to App Review with the product. While the product is with App Review, Ploa keeps the image and sends it itself once Apple has decided (the answer says so; nothing to retry). App Store only: Google Play keeps no image for a product. Needs a token allowed to submit.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_offers_get
tools.description: A subscription's offers as its store has them, each with its id, type, state (active, draft, scheduled, inactive, ended) and terms. App Store types: intro (the introductory offer, one per country, read as one: the free trial is one too), promotional (code is what the app signs), winback (who it's for under winback), code (offer codes; customers and how many codes were made). Google Play: offers on the base plan, with phases ({ duration, periods, kind: free | discount | price, percent, price }), eligibility (new_app, new_subscription, upgrade, developer), upgradeFrom and tags; trial is true for the free trial the product sets. Prices are US dollars. A Google Play productId is "product:basePlan".

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_offer_save
tools.description: Creates an offer on one subscription (leave offerId out), or changes or ends one (offerId from ploa_offers_get), straight to the store (needs a token allowed to submit). End one with values { state: "ended" }; put a Google Play draft or ended offer on sale with { state: "active" }. App Store values: type (intro, promotional, winback, code), mode (free, pay_as_you_go, pay_up_front), duration (P3D P1W P2W P1M P2M P3M P6M P1Y; for pay_as_you_go the length of each period), periods (pay_as_you_go: 1 to 12), price (US dollars such as "0.99": Apple picks its nearest price point at or above and the equal price in every country); promotional: name and code (what the app signs); winback: name, code (its offer ID), paidMonths, sinceMonths [min, max], startDate (YYYY-MM-DD), optional endDate, waitMonths, priority (high, normal); code: name, customers (new, existing, expired), stackWithIntro. A new intro replaces the one there, the free trial too, country by country: it answers with a job that ploa_product_job follows (offerId "intro" changes or ends it). Only a promotional offer's price and a win-back's dates, priority and months change later; offer codes only end. Google Play values: code (the offer ID: lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens), phases (one or two: [{ duration such as P7D or P1M, periods, kind: free | discount | price, percent (1-99) or price }]; Play allows one paid phase, so two are a free one then a paid one), eligibility (new_app, new_subscription, upgrade with upgradeFrom another subscription's product ID or empty for another base plan of this one, developer: only when the app asks for it), tags. On a base plan already on sale a new offer goes on sale at once; otherwise with the plan. From an agent, a new offer, a price, phases or putting one on sale wait for a person's approval; ending and the rest go straight through.

offerId.description: The offer to change or end; leave out to create.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_offer_codes
tools.description: The codes of one App Store offer code (offerId "code:…" from ploa_offers_get). action list: its batches of one-time codes and its custom codes, each with an id, count, expiry and whether it still works. action create (values { kind: one_time | custom, count, expires: YYYY-MM-DD, customCode for custom }): one-time codes (up to 25,000 a batch) Apple makes in a few minutes, or one custom code people type (count is how many times it can be redeemed); from an agent this waits for a person's approval. action download (batchId of one-time codes, saveTo an absolute path for the CSV file): writes the codes to that file and says how many; it never prints them. action end (batchId): those codes stop working.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_revenuecat_create_product
tools.description: Creates a product the store already has in the app's RevenueCat project, under the same identifier so purchases unlock what they should, and optionally adds it to an entitlement and to a package of the current offering. values: platform (ios or android), storeId (the store's product ID; a Google Play subscription is "product:basePlan"), kind (subscription, consumable, non_consumable), displayName, entitlementId and packageId (from ploa_revenuecat_product_options). Always waits for a person's approval when an agent asks.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_revenuecat_product_options
tools.description: The RevenueCat project's entitlements and the packages of its current offering, with the IDs ploa_revenuecat_create_product takes.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_sales
tools.description: This app's downloads from each store's daily reports: first-time downloads (Google Play: new users) and updates for the last 30 days, against the 30 days before, with a value per day for 60 days. Also each store page's funnel: App Store impressions, product page views, downloads by source, conversion, sessions and deletions (from Apple's analytics reports, once a person has started them), and Play's store listing visitors and acquisitions by traffic source. For tokens of the workspace's owners, also Apple's proceeds and Google's earnings per currency and RevenueCat's numbers; anyone else's token gets downloads only. A store whose reports can't be read says what to set up (the App Store vendor number and a key role that can read sales, or the Play reports bucket and permission). Reports are daily, so answers are kept for hours.

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_testflight_get
tools.description: The app's TestFlight as App Store Connect has it: tester groups (internal or external, how many testers, the public link and its limit, which builds each has; an internal group may get every build on its own), the beta information Apple's beta review needs (description and feedback email per language) and the beta review contact (the demo password is never shown, only whether one is set), and what is still missing before a build can go to beta review. With buildId (from ploa_release_status or the store's builds), that build's side too: What to Test per language, the groups that have it, its beta review state and its export compliance answer. With groupId, the group's testers and where each stands (invited, accepted, installed).

dir.description: The app's folder (absolute path). Defaults to the folder the agent runs in.

tools.name: ploa_testflight_save
tools.description: One TestFlight change, straight to App Store Connect (needs a token allowed to submit). values by action — group.create: { name, internal (bool), allBuilds (bool, internal groups) }. group.update: { groupId, name, feedback (bool), allBuilds (bool, internal groups: every build on its own), publicLink (bool, external groups), publicLinkLimit (number or null) }. group.delete: { groupId }. testers.add: { groupId, testers: [{ email, firstName, lastName }] }: Apple emails each one, so from an agent it waits for a person's approval. testers.remove: { groupId, testerIds }. build.whatToTest: { buildId, text, locale (default the app's primary language) }. build.groups: { buildId, add: [groupId], remove: [groupId] } (an external group gets a build once beta review approved it). build.encryption: { buildId, usesNonExemptEncryption }. build.submitBeta: { buildId, label }: sends the build to beta review so external testers can have it; from an agent it waits for a person's approval, and it needs the beta information first. info: { locale, description, feedbackEmail, marketingUrl, privacyPolicyUrl }. review: { contactFirstName, contactLastName, contactPhone, contactEmail, demoAccountRequired, demoAccountName, demoAccountPassword, notes }.

tools.name: ploa_play_testers_get
tools.description: Google Play's testing tracks as Play has them: internal testing, closed testing (alpha and any closed track of the app's own naming) and open testing, each with the release on it now (name, version codes, status) and, for internal and closed tracks, its tester Google Groups. Play's API knows testers only as Google Groups: Play Console's email lists (the only kind internal testing takes there) aren't in it, and open testing has no list. Also the opt-in link testers join through and the app's Play Console IDs. testersError says why the groups couldn't be read (Play's daily edit limit for the app, mostly). Kept for 10 minutes; fresh asks Play again, which may use one of the app's daily edits.

Each store's ratings summary too (the App Store's own average and count; for Google Play, the average of the reviews read). Google Play gives only reviews with text from about the last week; older ones are only in Play Console. Filter by store, stars (a list such as [1, 2]) and unanswered.

Write it as the app's developer: thank, answer the point, no promises the team hasn't made. From an agent it waits for a person's approval (needs a token allowed to submit).

Apple's API gives no test results (impressions, conversion, improvement): those are only in App Store Connect › Product Page Optimization. Google Play's custom store listings and store listing experiments have no API: they are made in Play Console.

(leave out to add), name, appIconName? }; test.treatmentRemove { testId, treatmentId }; test.locale { testId, treatmentId, locale } (then upload its screenshots); test.remove { testId }; test.review { testId }; test.start { testId } (once App Review approved it); test.stop { testId } (it can't start again); media.remove { owner: page|test, parentId, localizationId, kind: screenshot|preview, id }; media.order { owner, parentId, localizationId, kind, setId, ids }. The file is checked against the store's rules first (ploa_screenshot_specs, ploa_screenshot_check) and refused with the reasons if the store wouldn't take it. Ploa shows the project's icon until a store shows a newer one, and puts it (at 512×512) on a Google Play listing that has no icon yet; one Play already has stays. Other Ploa tools already send a changed icon on the way; use this right after changing it, or to fill a new app's Play listing icon.

tools.name: ploa_app_links
tools.description: Makes links to the app's web open the app itself: writes .well-known/apple-app-site-association (iOS Universal Links) and .well-known/assetlinks.json (Android App Links) into the web project's public folder (public/, Flutter's web/), from what Ploa knows: the bundle ID and the Apple team of the App Store connection, the package name and the SHA-256 of the upload key Ploa keeps. Google Play re-signs every install with its own app signing key, so pass that key's SHA-256 too (androidFingerprints): the person reads it in Play Console › Test and release › App integrity › App signing; links don't open the app from Play installs without it. paths: the paths the app opens (default every path, "*"; "/invite/*" opens only those). The files go live with the next ploa_web_build. The answer says what the app's own config needs (Expo: ios.associatedDomains and android.intentFilters with autoVerify); Ploa turns on Associated Domains at Apple when the build's entitlements ask for it. Only on the MCP server on this computer.

androidFingerprints.description: SHA-256 fingerprints of Google Play's app signing key (Play Console › App integrity › App signing), in any form (AB:CD:… or plain hex).

tools.name: ploa_web_status
tools.description: The workspace's web on Ploa's hosting (Ploa Aio), each the web app or site of one app: its address, what it is (a web app, pages about the app, or both; installable as a PWA), and its versions with where each stands (going up, with testers at its testing address, waiting for a person to approve its release, live, replaced), Ploa's checks on each, and the hosting room. Read-only. Start here.

site.description: The site's address (the part before .ploa.app) or ID. Needed when the workspace has more than one site.

tools.name: ploa_web_setup
tools.description: Adds the web to one of the person's apps, at a free <address>.ploa.app, or changes what an app's web is. kind: 'app' (the app itself in the browser), 'site' (pages about the app, linking to its store apps) or 'both' (the pages at the address, the web app under /app); pwa: installable to the home screen. An app with store apps on both platforms needs no PWA on phones (people should get the store apps): leave pwa off unless the person wants it on computers, and then point phones at the stores (the manifest's prefer_related_applications with its Google Play app, and Apple's apple-itunes-app smart banner meta; Ploa's check 'storesFirst' says what's missing). An app with no store apps can be web only. Ask the person which address they want and what the web is; don't pick for them. Ploa sells no domains: a domain they own connects later (ploa_web_domain_add).

tools.name: ploa_web_build
tools.description: Builds the web app or site in this project with its own framework's command and sends it as a new version. Ploa knows Expo (npx expo export --platform web), Next.js with output: 'export', Astro, SvelteKit with adapter-static, Nuxt (generate), React Router in SPA mode, Angular, Gatsby, Docusaurus, VitePress, Eleventy, Vite, Create React App, Vue CLI, Hugo, Jekyll, MkDocs, Flutter (flutter build web), any project with a build script, and plain HTML; it installs the packages first when they're missing, and finds the output folder (out, dist, build, .output/public, build/web...). A project set up to run a server (Next without output: 'export', Astro's server output, SvelteKit's server adapters, Remix with SSR) is refused with how to make it static: Ploa hosts static files for now. build: false sends what's built already (pass dir for the built folder). Ploa numbers it (the version from app.json or package.json, and a build number it counts), checks it (every file it asks for, no keys or .env, no form sending a password elsewhere, the room, phones, sharing, the PWA's manifest and the store links), and puts it at its own testing address (<site>--<build>.ploa.app) for the site's testers. Nothing goes live: ploa_web_release does, once the person says it's good. Files like .env, .git and node_modules are never sent. The site's own rules go in a ploa.json beside package.json (or in the built folder): rewrites ({from: '/he/*', to: '/he.html'}), redirects, headers (Content-Security-Policy, Cache-Control and a few more) and a proxy sending a path to the site's own API ({from: '/api/*', to: 'https://api.example.com', strip: true}), which Ploa allows only to a domain connected and proven with ploa_web_domain_add.

Without changes it only reads them.

Like production in the stores, it needs a person: this only asks, and the person approves on ploa.dev (ploa_approval_status tells you), unless ploa_access says you're autonomous, when it goes at once. Never try another way around the approval.

tools.name: ploa_web_domain_add
tools.description: Connects a domain the person already owns (example.com or www.example.com) to one of their sites. Ploa sells no domains: every site has its free <address>.ploa.app, and the plan limits how many own domains connect (Free: none; Starter 1, Pro 3, Team any). Returns the DNS records the person adds where their domain's DNS is managed: a TXT that proves it's theirs, and an A record (bare domain) or CNAME (subdomain) to Ploa. Give the person the records exactly; don't change their DNS for them unless they ask. Then ploa_web_domain_check.
